parts.textTemplate: The handshake is one of the oldest greetings in the world. Historians believe it began (1)___ ancient times as a way (2)___ show that a person was not carrying a weapon. By offering an open hand, two strangers could prove (3)___ they meant no harm to each other. Over the centuries, the gesture spread across many cultures and became (4)___ standard way of greeting someone in business and social situations. Today, a firm handshake is often seen (5)___ a sign of confidence, while a weak one can leave a negative impression. In some countries, however, physical greetings like handshakes are becoming less common, and many people now prefer a simple nod or wave instead. Whether this trend (6)___ continue or the handshake will remain popular for centuries to come is difficult to predict.

parts.title: Part 2 — Multiple Matching
parts.skillNote: To'rtta qisqa matn (A-D) beriladi. Har bir gap qaysi matnga tegishli ekanini aniqlang. Diqqat: bir matn bir necha marta ishlatilishi mumkin.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Amira
texts.text: Amira runs a small graphic design studio from her home in Termiz. She started freelancing five years ago and now works with clients across Central Asia. She says the hardest part of running her own business was learning to manage her time, since nobody was telling her what to do each day. She now uses a strict weekly schedule and never works on Sundays, no matter how much work is waiting.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Sardor
texts.text: Sardor manages a logistics company that delivers goods between Surkhandarya and Tashkent. He took over the business from his father ten years ago and has since doubled the number of trucks. His biggest challenge has been finding reliable drivers, so he now offers extra training and a bonus system to keep good employees from leaving for competitors.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Nilufar
texts.text: Nilufar co-founded an online marketplace for local farmers to sell their produce directly to city customers, cutting out expensive middlemen. In the beginning, many farmers were suspicious of selling online and preferred traditional markets. Nilufar spent months visiting villages in person to explain how the platform worked before farmers started trusting it.

texts.label: D
texts.title: Bekzod
texts.text: Bekzod opened a language center offering English and business courses in his hometown. Demand grew so quickly that within a year he had to move to a bigger building and hire three more teachers. He believes the key to his success has been word-of-mouth recommendations from satisfied students rather than paid advertising.

parts.title: Part 3 — Multiple Choice
parts.skillNote: Uzun matnni o'qib, har bir savol uchun eng to'g'ri javobni tanlang.
parts.text:
The Four-Day Work Week: A Passing Trend or the Future of Work?

Over the past few years, a growing number of companies around the world have experimented with a four-day work week, giving employees a three-day weekend without cutting their pay. Supporters of the idea point to trial programs in which companies reported little or no drop in productivity, and in some cases even saw improvements, as employees returned to work more rested and motivated. Workers in these trials also reported lower stress levels and better relationships at home, since they had more time for family, hobbies, and rest.

However, not everyone believes the model can work for every type of business. Critics argue that the four-day week is easiest to introduce in office-based jobs where tasks can be reorganized flexibly, but far more difficult in industries such as healthcare, manufacturing, or retail, where someone must always be present to serve customers or operate machinery. For these industries, a four-day week would likely mean hiring additional staff, which increases costs significantly.

Another concern raised by economists is that shorter trials, often lasting only a few months, may not reveal the full picture. Employees might work harder during a trial simply because they know they are being observed, a phenomenon researchers call the “observer effect”. Whether the same productivity levels would be maintained over several years remains uncertain, and few companies have committed to the four-day model on a permanent, long-term basis.

Despite these doubts, several governments have begun studying the idea more seriously, and a handful of countries have launched national pilot programs. Whether the four-day week becomes standard practice or remains a niche experiment limited to a small number of progressive companies is a question that will likely take years, not months, to answer.

parts.text:
From Market Stall to National Brand: The Story of Uzbek Honey

Twelve years ago, Farida began selling homemade honey from a small stall at her local bazaar in Surkhandarya. She had learned beekeeping from her grandfather as a child and always believed the family's honey was special. (21)___ Still, she had never imagined turning it into a full business.

The turning point came when a customer, impressed by the quality, asked whether she could supply honey to a small shop in Tashkent. (22)___ Farida agreed, even though she had no experience shipping products such a long distance.

The first shipment sold out within a week. (23)___ Encouraged by this success, Farida began looking for more shops willing to stock her honey.

Growing the business was not easy. (24)___ She had to learn how to negotiate prices, handle paperwork, and ensure her packaging met national safety standards.

A major challenge came when a large supermarket chain expressed interest in her product. (25)___ Farida realized she would need to significantly increase her production capacity.

She decided to hire her first employees, two local women experienced in food processing. (26)___ Together, they built a small production facility behind Farida's house.

Within two years, the business had grown enough to require a proper factory. (27)___ Farida took out a small loan to fund the move, which she paid back within eighteen months.

Today, Farida's honey is sold in shops across the country, and she employs twelve people full-time. (28)___ She credits her grandfather's early lessons for giving her both the skill and the confidence to start.

Looking back, Farida says she never expected her small bazaar stall to grow into a national brand. (29)___ Her advice to other young entrepreneurs is simple: start small, but always be ready to grow.

parts.text:
Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Workplace

Artificial intelligence, once mostly discussed in science fiction, has quietly become part of everyday working life. Tools that can draft emails, analyze spreadsheets, or answer customer questions are now common in offices of all sizes, from small family businesses to multinational corporations. Supporters argue that these tools free employees from repetitive tasks, allowing them to focus on more creative or strategic work that machines cannot easily replicate.

At the same time, the rapid spread of these technologies has raised concerns among workers, particularly in roles that involve large amounts of routine data processing or basic writing. Some economists predict that certain jobs will disappear entirely over the next decade, while others believe that, as with previous waves of technological change, new types of jobs will emerge to replace the ones that are lost. History offers some support for this second view: the introduction of computers in the 1980s eliminated many clerical positions but created entirely new fields, such as software development and IT support, that did not previously exist.

What makes the current transition different, according to some researchers, is its speed. Earlier technological shifts often unfolded over several decades, giving workers and educational institutions time to adapt gradually. Artificial intelligence tools, by contrast, have become widely available within just a few years, leaving many companies and employees scrambling to catch up. Training programs that once took years to design and approve are now being rushed into place, sometimes with mixed results.

For businesses in developing economies, including many in Central Asia, the situation presents both a challenge and an opportunity. Companies that adopt these tools early may gain a significant advantage over slower competitors, particularly in industries like customer service, logistics, and translation. However, without proper training and investment, there is also a risk that the benefits of these technologies will be concentrated among a small number of large firms, leaving smaller businesses further behind.

Most experts agree on one point: simply avoiding these tools is not a realistic long-term strategy for most businesses. The more useful question, they suggest, is not whether to adopt artificial intelligence, but how to do so in a way that supports employees rather than replacing them entirely.
